title: Closures, capture, and the loop-with-var trap
hook: A closure is a function that remembers the variables from the place it was created, even after that outer function has finished. That power drives factories and callbacks — and the loop-with-var trap breaks production code when you confuse scope chain with call stack.

blocks.text: A **closure** is the combination of a function plus the lexical environment it closes over. When an inner function references an outer variable, the engine keeps that binding alive in the outer environment as long as any inner function might still run. **Capture** means the inner function reads (and often mutates) a variable from an enclosing scope. Closures are not a special syntax — every nested function that touches an outer local is a closure.

entries.plainDefinition: A function that retains access to its outer lexical environment after the outer function returns.
When an inner function references a binding from an outer scope, keeping that binding reachable.
Creating closures in a for loop with var shares one binding; all callbacks see the final value.
entries.example: for (var i=0; i<3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0); // 3,3,3

entries.plainDefinition: Linked outer environments used for lookup — distinct from the call stack of executing frames.
entries.example: Callback resolves i via the loop's shared var binding, not via call order.

blocks.text: Closures power module patterns, event handlers, React hooks, debounce/throttle, and partial application. They also cause memory leaks when a long-lived callback captures a large DOM subtree or request object. The **loop-with-var trap** is the most cited JavaScript interview puzzle on Reddit: three `setTimeout` callbacks all log `3` because `var i` is one function-scoped binding mutated each iteration. `let` creates a per-iteration binding; an IIFE (Immediately Invoked Function Expression) snapshot works too.

blocks.title: Scope chain vs call stack — again
blocks.body: When the timeout fires, the call stack shows the timer callback. Variable lookup still walks the scope chain to the environment where the arrow was created — often a shared loop binding if you used var.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Define inner function
items.body: The engine records [[Environment]] pointing at the current outer lexical environment.

items.title: Reference outer binding
items.body: Any free variable resolves through the scope chain at run time, not at definition time for const/let values.

items.title: Outer function returns
items.body: If the inner function is still reachable, the outer environment stays alive in the heap.

items.title: Invoke later
items.body: Call stack pushes the inner frame; scope chain still links to captured environments.

blocks.title: Closures across languages
rows: foreach captures loop variable per iteration (since C# 5)

blocks.title: Closures in loops with var
blocks.body: Event listeners, setTimeout, and Promise factories inside for (var i...) almost always need let, an IIFE parameter, or a factory function call per iteration.

blocks.title: Accidental memory retention
blocks.body: A debounce handler that closes over a 5 MB parsed JSON tree keeps that tree alive until the handler is garbage-collected. Pass IDs, not whole graphs.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: Chrome DevTools Memory → take heap snapshot → filter Closure or search retained size after navigating away. Detached DOM nodes with click handlers that captured `element` or `componentState` are the classic leak. For the loop trap, paste the var version in a live coding pad — interviewers expect you to draw two columns: **call stack** (who executes now) vs **scope chain** (where `i` lives). V8 allocates a context object per closure; capturing three locals in one inner function typically shares one context, not three separate copies of the function.

snippet.explanation: Line 5: production bug — three registered handlers share i. Line 11: let gives each arrow its own i binding; network tab shows /0, /1, /2.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Harder to inspect; leak risk if long-lived

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying closures copy variable values at creation time for let/var loop counters — they close over bindings, and var shares one. Claiming scope chain and call stack are the same structure. Answering the loop puzzle with 'use bind' without explaining why var fails. Not mentioning memory leaks when asked where closures hurt production.

interviewTakeaways: A closure = function + retained lexical environment; capture keeps outer bindings alive on the heap.
loop-with-var: one shared binding → callbacks see final i; let creates per-iteration environments.
Scope chain resolves variables; call stack orders execution — draw both when explaining async loop output.
60s: Inner function closes over outer vars via [[Environment]]. var in loops shares one i. let or IIFE snapshot fixes it. Long-lived closures can leak DOM and large objects.
Follow-up: implement once() or a counter using closure — no global state.
commonPitfalls: Weak: 'closures copy values' — they close over bindings; mutating a captured object is visible to all closures sharing it.
Weak: blaming setTimeout for the loop bug — the bug is var scope, not the timer.
Strong: 'Walk scope chain at callback time. var is function-scoped so one i. let is per-iteration. Profile heap for retained closures on SPAs.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: C# compiler emits a display class for captured locals. JavaScript engines use context objects similarly. C# foreach fixed loop capture in C# 5; JavaScript needs let.
TypeScript infers closure types from outer const/let. Captured mutable state needs careful typing when returning handlers from hooks.
